Goldbach's Conjecture. Every even integer greater than two can be expressed as the sum of two primes. Posed by the Prussian mathematician Christian Goldbach in 1742, this conjecture has resisted proof for over two centuries despite computational verification for numbers up to astronomical magnitudes, making it one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics. For instance, four equals two plus two, six equals three plus three, eight equals three plus five, ten equals five plus five, twelve equals five plus seven, and fourteen equals seven plus seven. Computational searches have verified the conjecture for all even numbers greater than two up to extremely large values, exceeding ten to the power of eighteen, yet a general proof remains out of reach. A related weaker version states that every odd number greater than five is the sum of three odd primes. This weak version was proven in 2013 by Harald Helfgott, a significant breakthrough. The conjecture illustrates how some of the most important problems in mathematics can be deceptively simple to state, yet profoundly difficult to prove. It connects to other famous unsolved questions about primes, particularly the Twin Prime Conjecture, which asks whether infinitely many pairs of primes differing by two exist. Both are fundamental open questions about prime distribution and gaps. The Prime Number Theorem provides context on overall prime density relevant to understanding Goldbach's frequencies, while the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic distinguishes the primes whose additive combinations are being questioned.
